name: Embedded System

claims.claim_text: The field dates from the first microprocessor in 1971 and the first eight-bit part a year later, and people entering then learned digital design and software on the job because nobody at their companies knew either.
claims.quote_verbatim: the 4004, the first micro, came out in 1971. And the 8008 was the first 8-bitder
claims.speaker: Jack Ganssle
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jack Ganssle - Embedded Elchee Epexegesis

claims.claim_text: Trade press coverage implies that anything below a fast 32-bit part is obsolete, which misrepresents the market.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you're not doing 32 bits at 500 megahertz, you're some sort of dinosaur
claims.speaker: Jack Ganssle
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jack Ganssle - Embedded Elchee Epexegesis

claims.claim_text: Small parts sell in the billions per year into applications where the entire program occupies hundreds of words of memory, which is why the predicted disappearance of the eight-bit microcontroller has failed to happen for two decades.
claims.quote_verbatim: literally hundreds of words of memory is the entire app
claims.speaker: Jack Ganssle
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jack Ganssle - Embedded Elchee Epexegesis

claims.claim_text: A large share of microcontroller customers are not software engineers but domain experts, in motor control or a similar field, writing a few hundred words of program and wanting something simple; cheap small processors keep opening applications nobody had imagined.
claims.quote_verbatim: a lot of their customers are not software people. They're domain experts. They're experts at motor control or something
claims.speaker: Jack Ganssle

claims.claim_text: A working embedded practice can sit entirely at 60 megahertz and below, where half a megabyte of RAM is more than the application knows what to do with and a few hundred kilobytes of flash is a great deal of code.
claims.quote_verbatim: Under 60 megahertz or 60 megahertz and below. If I see a half meg of RAM, I have no idea what to do with it
claims.speaker: Elecia White
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Elecia White - Wirewove Worshipping Wookieist?

claims.claim_text: Robotics work can go without a real-time operating system because its latency is not worth paying for, and in audio and visual effects work you at minimum have to know what the operating system is doing underneath you.
claims.quote_verbatim: We don't have an RTOS because the RTOS's latency just isn't worth it to us
claims.speaker: Elecia White
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Elecia White - Wirewove Worshipping Wookieist?

claims.claim_text: The recurring misconception from outside the field is that anything running in a browser should run on an embedded target, along with comparisons to old game consoles that ignore how tightly that code had to be written.
claims.quote_verbatim: People think that because it runs on Java in my browser window, it should easily be able to run on my embedded platform
claims.speaker: Elecia White
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Elecia White - Wirewove Worshipping Wookieist?

claims.claim_text: The recommended route in for an engineer from another discipline is to buy a development board and build a robot with it.
claims.quote_verbatim: Buy an Arduino and make a robot
claims.speaker: Elecia White
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Elecia White - Wirewove Worshipping Wookieist?

claims.claim_text: Beginner platforms present a false appearance of simplicity by concealing complexity, which is fine for starting out but leaves you with nowhere to stand the moment something needs fixing.
claims.quote_verbatim: they are trying to gloss over complexity in false indication of simplicity
claims.speaker: Piotr Esden-Tempski

claims.claim_text: Learning embedded work bottom up, starting from how registers behave, is separate from learning to program, and it is what makes it possible to reason about a system that is not doing what you expect.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you know what is going on under the hood, it's much easier to reason about it when it is not doing what you think it should
claims.speaker: Piotr Esden-Tempski

claims.claim_text: Abstraction is the standard way to manage complexity in general computing but works against you here, because the details underneath keep surfacing and affecting behaviour you have to account for.
claims.quote_verbatim: for embedded systems, you need to know things because they bubble up from the bottom and really hit you
claims.speaker: Ken Tindell
claims.episode_title: The CAN bus can! with Dr Ken Tindell

claims.claim_text: Code produced by following a convention without examining it has been found to run four or five times the size of the application itself, which translates into a larger microcontroller in every unit and becomes a multi-million-dollar decision at automotive volumes.
claims.quote_verbatim: You're talking kind of four or five times the size of the application
claims.speaker: Ken Tindell
claims.episode_title: The CAN bus can! with Dr Ken Tindell

claims.claim_text: The organisational problem behind that is that engineering decisions rarely carry a visible cost, because purchasing and engineering sit in separate parts of the company.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's very, very hard to make sure the engineering decisions have a kind of a dollar cost attached to them
claims.speaker: Ken Tindell
claims.episode_title: The CAN bus can! with Dr Ken Tindell

claims.claim_text: Embedded work lets you reason down to first principles: the registers are visible and everything above them is under your control, whereas a web stack is built on other people's abstractions with correspondingly more places for something to be wrong.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you're working on embedded system, you can you can say, OK, well, I can look at the registers and then pretty much everything above that is under my control
claims.speaker: Andrew Seddon
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Andrew Seddon - Necessary Networked Novelty

claims.claim_text: Debugging is hard because the object under test is a complete system rather than a circuit or a desktop program: firmware is now large, it runs across several parts, and pieces can be broken through no fault of yours, down to a mislabelled component.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's a complete system with all these parts and memories and huge

claims.claim_text: As a system grows the temptation is to change variables and re-run to see whether it works; deliberately slowing down and recording what was tried both forces thought beforehand and leaves a log of the attempts.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you slow down and actually capture this stuff, it makes for better debugging
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: What defines an engineer? - Job Judging Jeremiad

claims.claim_text: One practical debugging habit is to use whatever output the product already has as the instrument, displaying variables on the product's own screen or indicator rather than reaching for external equipment.
claims.quote_verbatim: if it has an LCD, I'll use the LCD for debugging
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: What defines an engineer? - Job Judging Jeremiad

claims.claim_text: Newcomers from software connect a logic analyser to a running board, see an idle bus and conclude nothing is happening; the traffic they wanted occurred during boot, and pressing reset makes it appear.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's an embedded system. So it's done booting. So it's spit something out at the very beginning
claims.speaker: Dmitry Nedospasov
claims.episode_title: Impedance Matching with Michael Ossmann and Dmitry Nedospazov

claims.claim_text: Zephyr brings Linux-style configuration and a large body of existing, pre-written components to real-time embedded work, at the cost of pulling down every vendor SDK it supports, which runs to tens of gigabytes.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's basically, it's kind of like Linux for embedded
claims.speaker: Jared Wolff

claims.claim_text: Connected products are systems of systems demanding embedded, security, RF, protocol, cloud and mobile expertise at once, and even a fully staffed team has nobody who is expert at the joins: writing the backend update service requires understanding how the device performs its own firmware handshake.
claims.quote_verbatim: every part of building an IoT product requires understanding at least the seams between the systems
claims.speaker: Jonathan Beri
claims.episode_title: Why IoT Is Difficult with Jonathan Beri

claims.claim_text: Customers who insist a few dozen bytes per message is too small are usually sending text-encoded structures; packing the same information as bits removes the constraint entirely.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can put quite a lot of data in there if you do it efficiently
claims.speaker: Maarten Engelen

claims.claim_text: On a combined processor and fabric device, a safety path running from a custom peripheral through bare-metal code into Linux and back carries real timing cost, and the design questions are buffer depth, how often the operating system services the interface, and what happens to accumulated data when the call does not come.
claims.quote_verbatim: then you got to consider like what your buffer size is, like how frequency is Linux serving this servicing this thing? What happens if like that call never comes
claims.speaker: Ryan Cousins

claims.claim_text: The compensating advantage of that integration is that the link between the programmable fabric and the processor cores is never the bottleneck, unlike a design that has to serialise data between two separate chips.
claims.quote_verbatim: communication bandwidth is never an issue between the FPGA and the ARM cores
claims.speaker: Ryan Cousins

claims.claim_text: In a memory-safe language targeting hardware, even writing to a peripheral register counts as unsafe under the memory model, so unsafe blocks are unavoidable rather than a sign of bad code, and the skill is knowing the practices that make them correct.
claims.quote_verbatim: even just running to a register might be considered unsafe just for, for how the memory model works
claims.speaker: Laura Abbott
claims.episode_title: Finding Hardware Flaws with Laura Abbott

claims.claim_text: A full standard library ported to a small wireless part gives threads and mutexes rather than a stripped-down environment, which was enough to write a stable power-monitoring watchdog for a main processor in a couple of hundred lines.
claims.quote_verbatim: develop a fairly simple, you know, power ons monitoring, you know, watched a kind of system for a main processor on this little ESP 32 C3 in a couple hundred lines
claims.speaker: Ariel Briner

claims.claim_text: Deferred logging avoids the classic cost of print debugging: the format strings are never compiled into the binary, only symbols, so the device transmits a few bytes of pointer instead of spending flash space and serial time on text.
claims.quote_verbatim: there's a Rust library that lets you do all these logging prints, but they don't get compiled into the binary. It's just kind of symbols
claims.speaker: Ariel Briner

claims.claim_text: Firmware remains C with some assembly and C++ and is unlikely to move soon, and where cost is not the binding constraint an inexpensive 32-bit ARM part is hard to argue against unless the design specifically needs programmable logic.
claims.quote_verbatim: why don't you just use, you know, that cheap 32 bit arm or whatever
claims.speaker: Jeremiah Gillis

claims.claim_text: Hardware deliverables are governed by long-established quality processes while firmware quality is the weaker side of the same consultancy, and the framing that helps is treating firmware as professional work with the same delivery expectations.
claims.quote_verbatim: the firmware is an area that I'm working on, you know, more and more and I, and I want to do better with that

claims.claim_text: Verification in embedded work is still often subjective bench observation rather than automated testing, and practices such as continuous integration arrived late because the field is old enough to have settled habits.
claims.quote_verbatim: I'm used to running the unit test for me is I'm on my bench and I'm like, oh yeah, look at that
claims.episode_title: Firmware Deployment and Troubleshooting with Akbar Dhanaliwala

claims.claim_text: Hardware security work uses the instruments engineers already own, oscilloscopes, logic analysers, supplies, programmers and debug interfaces, so the shift required is one of perspective rather than equipment: asking how the interfaces that help you can be used against you.
claims.quote_verbatim: how can the hacker use these interfaces that are helpful to me against me
claims.speaker: Joe Grand
claims.episode_title: New Life Skills with Joe Grand

claims.claim_text: Every industry that makes a physical good is somewhere along the curve of putting microcontrollers into it, which means the security surface now follows the embedded system wherever it goes, consumer or industrial.
claims.quote_verbatim: any place there's an embedded system, there's a potential security problem
claims.speaker: Michael Ossmann
claims.episode_title: A Security Update with Michael Ossmann

claims.claim_text: On a launch vehicle a single compute node with all the sensors and actuators wired to it is not a viable architecture, so the design starts by classifying which kinds of problem exist before choosing hardware.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's not feasible to just have like a single embedded, like compute device with all of the sensors and all of the actuators plugged into like, you know, a single CPU or processor
claims.speaker: Charles Aylward
claims.episode_title: Software for Rockets with Charles Aylward

claims.claim_text: A measurement instrument that replaced a rack of bench equipment was built on a processor module with external SRAM rather than a microcontroller, chosen for deterministic timing across many serial ports and interrupt sources.
claims.quote_verbatim: you had the deterministic timing and all the rest of it
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: That entire development ended in a production run of ten units, which is a common shape for instrumentation work and worth knowing before committing to a custom design.
claims.quote_verbatim: we only ended up making a run of 10 of them
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: A managed-runtime embedded platform's smallest achievable footprint was 64 kilobytes of RAM regardless of what the program did, since that figure was almost entirely runtime overhead.
claims.quote_verbatim: You can get it down to 64 K of Ram. That's what he said is the smallest you can get it to be
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: A Linux-class single-board computer is a poor default for an embedded application on power grounds alone, needing five volts at a couple of amps where the job may not justify it.
claims.quote_verbatim: five volts or two and a half amps, thank you very much
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Bit-banged timing off a Linux board's general-purpose pins that just about worked on earlier hardware fails on newer boards, because the path to the pins is both slower and far more variable once other bus traffic contends with it; dedicated programmable I/O is the fix.
claims.quote_verbatim: your latency is higher to the GPIO and it's also more variable
claims.episode_title: The RP1 and beyond with the Raspberry Pi Hardware team

claims.claim_text: A prototype-level board cannot simply be handed to a high-volume line: reaching volume means design optimisation for power and cost plus building test automation, which are prerequisites rather than afterthoughts.
claims.quote_verbatim: You can't have a prototype level board to be manufactured in very high volume setup
claims.speaker: Pallav Aggarwal

claims.claim_text: Rolling your own development board is no longer a business, because equivalents already exist far more cheaply; the workable model is building the hardware in support of teaching material and selling the content rather than the board.
claims.quote_verbatim: I'm going to make this board and then let's teach people how to make this board
claims.speaker: Shawn Hymel

claims.claim_text: A project with no hard price target and no hard specification accumulated features, never got certified and never shipped, which is the argument for imposing constraints on your own designs.
claims.quote_verbatim: it was not enough of a hard price target, enough of a hard spec target
claims.speaker: Shawn Hymel

claims.claim_text: Putting perception into a genuinely embedded device means running the vision workload on a dedicated chip and emitting only metadata, such as an object's coordinates in metres, over a simple serial link to a small microcontroller.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can have like an SPI output to, you know, an AT-Mega if you want, or to an ESP32
claims.speaker: Brandon Gilles
claims.episode_title: Depth and AI with Brandon Gilles and Brian Weinstein

claims.claim_text: Recognisable sentinel values are useful when scanning memory during troubleshooting, but on a very small system they consume bytes that the application needs.
claims.quote_verbatim: as you're looking down the memory and you see dead beef, it's a very recognizable thing
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: LED Designs, Last Minute Designs and Board Designs

claims.claim_text: The line people draw between a Linux machine and an embedded one is usually the memory management unit; task scheduling and interrupt-driven response are the same ideas at both scales.
claims.quote_verbatim: That's like the big definitive difference between like a Linux system and a embedded system
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Small programmable logic parts occupy the niche complex programmable logic once filled, offering lookup-table fabric and distributed RAM without signal-processing blocks, which suits connecting up assorted interfaces in an embedded design.
claims.quote_verbatim: they're pretty nice for doing embedded things and connecting up different IOs
claims.speaker: Luke Valenty

claims.claim_text: The actor model maps naturally onto embedded work because each unit is isolated and communicates by message rather than by shared state, which removes the usual difficulty of getting concurrent processes to talk.
claims.quote_verbatim: Erlang employs this model of concurrency called actor model where things are abstracted into their own individual units
claims.speaker: Omer Kilic

claims.claim_text: Large processor vendors have entered and left this market repeatedly, most recently by discontinuing a line of connected development boards, which is a reason to weigh vendor commitment when choosing a platform.
claims.quote_verbatim: Intel has gotten in and out of the embedded business like five times
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: A high-level language runtime is a reasonable entry point when its layers can be peeled back as needed, since the implementation underneath is open C that can be optimised by anyone with the skills.
claims.quote_verbatim: there are those layers that you can peel back as you find that you need to
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Memory modules returned by large customers come back as entire batches rather than individual failures, because one fault is treated as a threat to fleet reliability, which puts millions of dollars of leading-edge product at stake per incident.
claims.quote_verbatim: they don't just return that one module, they return the whole batch of them
claims.speaker: Nash Reilly

claims.claim_text: Even a simple vehicle accessory becomes a distributed system: nodes scattered through the vehicle each running their own logic while reporting state back to a controller that verifies all of them for safety.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's all of these nodes scattered in the vehicle and they all need to control their own logic, but also feedback to a motherboard that also verifies all of their states
claims.episode_title: Moving Down The Stack with Scott Williams

claims.claim_text: Industrial control taught through programmable logic controllers made no sense as classroom logic and only became clear on a factory floor, where the physical motion and audible feedback supplied the meaning the diagrams lacked.
claims.quote_verbatim: it clicked when I actually got into industry
claims.speaker: Don Wilcher
claims.episode_title: Engineering Education with Dr Don Wilcher

claims.claim_text: Developing against a soft processor is faster on the host first: the same scripts that read and write peripheral registers over a bridge can later run unchanged on the core itself, so the debugging conveniences of a full workstation are available until the code is right.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can do all your development on the host computer initially where you've got your full IDE
claims.speaker: Tim "Mithro" Ansell
